Company
KūM-p'-nē
n. (rendering Hebrew qāhāl, g'dūd, and tsābā', Greek sunodia and homilia)
From Old French compaignie, from Late Latin companio, one who eats bread (panis) with (cum) another — a companion is literally a bread-sharer. The etymology is worth keeping, because Scripture's warnings and commendations about company almost always concern the table: with such an one no not to eat, on the one hand; and on the other, the Lord Jesus receiving sinners and eating with them. To keep company is, in the oldest sense of the word, to share a loaf.

Biblical Definition

Company in Scripture means the persons a man travels, eats, and identifies with, and it is treated as a formative power rather than a neutral circumstance. The word can name a band of heralds, and in one striking verse the company that publishes the good news is a company of women: “The Lord gave the word: great was the company of those that published it” (Psa 68:11). It can name the ordinary travelling caravan, and the most sobering use in the Gospels is exactly that — Joseph and Mary lost the Lord Jesus by assuming He was among the familiar crowd: “But they, supposing him to have been in the company, went a day's journey; and they sought him among their kinsfolk and acquaintance” (Luk 2:44). It is possible to travel a full day in religious company and not have Christ in it, and the discovery is made only by looking for Him. Against every earthly company the epistle to the Hebrews sets the assembly the believer has already joined: “But ye are come unto mount Sion, and unto the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem, and to an innumerable company of angels” (Heb 12:22) — a present tense, not a future one. And the Old Testament's practical wisdom about company runs throughout: he that walketh with wise men shall be wise, but a companion of fools shall be destroyed. What a man consents to belong to, he becomes.

Webster 1828 Definition

An assembly or band of persons; those with whom one associates or travels; fellowship or companionship itself; and in Scripture the company that published the word, the caravan in which Christ was presumed but absent, and the innumerable company of angels believers have come to.

expand to see more

COMPANY, n. 1. Persons assembled together; an assemblage of persons for social or other purposes.

2. An assembly of persons associated for the transaction of business, or for the prosecution of some design.

3. Companionship; fellowship; society; the act of keeping with another. Evil communications corrupt good manners. 1 Cor. 15.

4. A band or body of soldiers; a subdivision of a regiment.

5. In Scripture, great was the company of those that published it. Psalm 68. An innumerable company of angels. Heb. 12.

Key Scripture

Psalm 68:11 — "The Lord gave the word: great was the company of those that published it."

Luke 2:44 — "But they, supposing him to have been in the company, went a day's journey; and they sought him among their kinsfolk and acquaintance."

Hebrews 12:22 — "But ye are come unto mount Sion, and unto the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem, and to an innumerable company of angels,"

Proverbs 11:14 — "Where no counsel is, the people fall: but in the multitude of counsellors there is safety."

Modern Corruption

The formative power of companionship is denied in the name of authenticity, so that warnings about evil company are dismissed as legalism, while the opposite error withdraws from sinners altogether and calls the withdrawal holiness.

expand to see more

The modern assumption is that a person's convictions are self-generated and therefore proof against his surroundings — that a man may keep any company he likes and remain what he is. Scripture flatly contradicts it: evil communications corrupt good manners, and a companion of fools shall be destroyed. The apostolic instruction is more specific still, and it concerns the table: Paul commands that with a professing brother who persists in gross sin the church is not to eat, precisely because shared bread signifies shared standing. To call such instruction legalism is to mistake a description of how human beings actually work for an arbitrary rule. Character is caught as much as taught, and the Bible treats the choice of companions as one of the most consequential a young man makes.

The opposite error hears these warnings and withdraws from the world entirely, treating separation from sinners as the substance of holiness. Paul anticipates and forbids the misreading in the same passage: he says he did not mean the fornicators of this world, for then must ye needs go out of the world — the discipline concerns those called a brother, not the unconverted. And the Lord Jesus bore the name of a friend of publicans and sinners without ever contracting their sin. The principle to recover is a double one: the church's table is guarded, and the Christian's life is not. A believer who cannot be found in the company of sinners has misunderstood his commission; a church which cannot say who may sit at the Supper has misunderstood its keys.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew qāhāl is an assembly or convocation; g'dūd is a troop or raiding band; tsābā' is a mustered host. Greek sunodia is a company travelling the same road, and homilia is association or intercourse, whence the warning of 1Co 15:33.

expand to see more

Hebrew qāhāl (H6951) — assembly, congregation, convocation; the gathered company of Israel before the LORD.

Hebrew g'dūd (H1416) — a band, troop, or raiding party; used of marauders and of David's men.

Greek sunodia (G4923) — a company journeying together, a caravan; the word in Luk 2:44, from sun (with) and hodos (way).

Greek homilia (G3657) — association, companionship, converse; evil communications corrupt good manners (1Co 15:33).

Greek munās / panegyris (G3831) — a festal gathering; paired with the innumerable company of angels in Heb 12:22-23.

Usage

"Of the heralds of the word: great was the company of those that published it (Psa 68:11)."

"Of Christ presumed present and absent: supposing him to have been in the company, went a day's journey (Luk 2:44)."

"Of the assembly believers have already joined: ye are come... to an innumerable company of angels (Heb 12:22)."
